n-vagus.summary: The cranial nerve with the widest distribution, giving parasympathetic fibres to most of the organs of the neck, chest and abdomen. It also supplies the muscles of the pharynx and larynx.
facts: Lateral groove of the medulla oblongata (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal nucleus of the vagus, nucleus of the solitary tract)

Leaves through the jugular foramen; in the neck it runs down in the carotid sheath with the carotid artery and internal jugular vein; in the chest it forms the oesophageal plexus and passes into the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus (anterior and posterior vagal trunks)

Muscles of the pharynx and palate (except tensor veli palatini), all muscles of the larynx (recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves); parasympathetic: heart, lungs and the digestive tract up to two thirds of the transverse colon
Lower larynx and pharynx, part of the external ear canal, visceral sensation from the thoracic and abdominal organs; taste from around the epiglottis
sections: It hooks under the subclavian artery on the right and the arch of the aorta on the left, rises in the groove between trachea and oesophagus and supplies all the muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid.
clinical: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (thyroidectomy, aortic aneurysm, lung tumour) causes hoarseness; bilateral damage causes respiratory distress.
In a vagus lesion the soft palate is pulled and the uvula deviates towards the healthy side.
Vasovagal syncope is fainting from bradycardia and hypotension caused by excessive vagal activity.
tus: Vagal fibres to the heart act more on the SA node on the right and on the AV node on the left.
The auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold's nerve) supplies part of the external ear canal; cleaning the ear can trigger a cough reflex.

n-accessorius.summary: The motor cranial nerve of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
facts: Its spinal roots come from the anterior horn of spinal cord segments C1–C5; it enters the skull through the foramen magnum
Leaves through the jugular foramen, pierces the sternocleidomastoid and crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to reach the trapezius
Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius
clinical: Because it lies superficially in the posterior triangle it can be injured during lymph node biopsy; the shoulder droops and shrugging is weak.
tus: The spinal root of the accessory nerve arises from the anterior horn of C1–C5, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen.

n-hypoglossus.summary: The motor nerve of the muscles of the tongue.
facts: Medulla oblongata (the groove between the pyramid and the olive)
Leaves through the hypoglossal canal, crosses the external carotid artery and enters the tongue on the outer surface of the hyoglossus
All the intrinsic muscles of the tongue and the genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus (but not the palatoglossus)
clinical: In a one-sided lower motor neuron lesion the protruded tongue deviates to the paralysed side, which shows atrophy and fasciculation.
It can be injured during carotid endarterectomy.
tus: The hypoglossal nerve crosses the external and internal carotid arteries on their lateral side; it can be injured in carotid endarterectomy.

plexus-brachialis.summary: The network of nerves formed by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C5–T1 that provides all the motor and sensory supply of the upper limb.
facts: Anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1 (roots)

Roots → trunks (superior, middle, inferior; in the scalene gap) → divisions (anterior/posterior; behind the clavicle) → cords (lateral, medial, posterior; around the axillary artery) → terminal branches
Terminal branches: musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, radial and axillary nerves; also the dorsal scapular, long thoracic, suprascapular, pectoral, subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves
Skin of the upper limb (medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm and others)
sections: Roots–Trunks–Divisions–Cords–Branches: 'Read That Damn Cadaver Book'. Lateral cord: musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of the median nerve; medial cord: ulnar nerve and medial root of the median nerve; posterior cord: axillary and radial nerves.
clinical: Erb–Duchenne palsy (upper trunk, C5–C6): from forcible separation of head and shoulder (birth, motorcycle accident) – the arm hangs at the side, internally rotated, with the forearm pronated ('waiter's tip' position).
Klumpke palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1): from a sudden upward pull on the arm – claw hand, sometimes with Horner syndrome.
Brachial plexus blocks (interscalene, supraclavicular, axillary) are used in upper limb surgery.
tus: The roots (C5–T1) and trunks of the brachial plexus lie in the posterior triangle of the neck, the cords in the axilla.
In avulsion at root level, Horner syndrome (T1) and involvement of the dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves indicate a preganglionic lesion.

n-musculocutaneus.summary: The nerve of the flexor muscles in the anterior compartment of the arm, which also gives sensation to the skin of the lateral forearm.
facts: Lateral cord (C5–C7)
Pierces the coracobrachialis and runs down between the biceps and brachialis; at the elbow it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis
Skin of the lateral side of the forearm
clinical: Isolated injury is rare; elbow flexion and supination are weak and the biceps reflex is lost.
tus: After musculocutaneous injury elbow flexion is partly kept by the brachioradialis; the biceps reflex is lost and sensation is lost on the lateral forearm.

n-axillaris.summary: The nerve of the deltoid and teres minor muscles, which also gives sensation to the outer side of the shoulder.
facts: Posterior cord (C5–C6)
Passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus
Deltoid, teres minor
Skin over the outer side of the shoulder (superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm – the 'regimental badge' area)
clinical: It is injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus and in shoulder dislocation: abduction of the arm is weak, the deltoid wastes and sensation is lost over the outer shoulder.
tus: The sensory branch of the axillary nerve is the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (the 'regimental badge' area).

n-radialis.summary: The largest branch of the brachial plexus, supplying all the extensor muscles of the posterior compartments of the arm and forearm.
facts: Posterior cord (C5–T1)
Spirals with the profunda brachii artery in the radial groove behind the humerus; in front of the elbow it divides into superficial (sensory) and deep (motor; posterior interosseous nerve) branches
Triceps brachii, anconeus, brachioradialis, wrist and finger extensors, supinator, the long muscles of the thumb
Back of the arm and forearm, lateral (radial) half of the back of the hand (first dorsal web space)
clinical: A fracture of the humeral shaft or prolonged pressure on the arm ('Saturday night palsy') causes wrist drop.
Damage to the posterior interosseous nerve causes finger drop without sensory loss.
Wrong use of a crutch can compress the nerve in the axilla.
tus: The radial nerve supplies all the extensors of the arm and forearm; its superficial branch carries sensation from the lateral half of the back of the hand.
Saturday night palsy: compression in the radial groove from the arm resting on the edge of a chair for a long time.

n-medianus.summary: The nerve of most forearm flexors and the thenar muscles of the hand, and the only nerve to pass through the carpal tunnel. It is called the 'eye of the hand' because it is essential for fine finger movements and fingertip sensation.
facts: Two roots from the lateral and medial cords (C5–T1)

Runs beside the brachial artery in the arm and lies medial to it in the cubital fossa; passes between the two heads of the pronator teres, runs down between FDS and FDP and enters the hand through the carpal tunnel

Forearm flexors (except FCU and the medial half of FDP), pronator teres and quadratus; in the hand the 'LOAF' muscles: 1st–2nd lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis
Lateral half of the palm, palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle and lateral half of the ring finger, and the backs of their tips
clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy: numbness worse at night, positive Tinel and Phalen tests, thenar wasting in advanced cases.
A lesion above the elbow gives the 'hand of benediction' (the index and middle fingers cannot be flexed).
It can be injured in wrist lacerations (suicide attempts) because it lies superficially there.
tus: The median nerve is the nerve of the 'hand and eye': thenar muscles, 1st–2nd lumbricals and palmar sensation of the lateral three and a half fingers.
Injury at the elbow gives the 'hand of benediction' (index and middle fingers cannot be flexed).

n-ulnaris.summary: The nerve that supplies most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand and gives sensation to the medial (little-finger) side of the hand. Because it lies under the skin at the elbow, a knock there causes the 'funny bone' feeling.
facts: Medial cord (C8–T1)
Runs down the medial side of the arm, passes in the groove behind the medial epicondyle, enters the forearm between the two heads of FCU and reaches the hand through Guyon's canal at the wrist
Flexor carpi ulnaris, medial half of FDP; in the hand the hypothenar muscles, 3rd–4th lumbricals, all interossei, adductor pollicis, deep head of FPB
Medial (ulnar) side of the hand: the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger
clinical: It can be trapped at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or at the wrist (Guyon's canal).
Injury causes a claw hand (4th–5th fingers), wasting of the interossei and a positive Froment sign.
It can be damaged in fractures of the medial epicondyle.
tus: The ulnar nerve is the nerve of fine hand movements: hypothenar muscles, interossei, 3rd–4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis.
It carries palmar and dorsal sensation from the medial one and a half fingers.

n-phrenicus.summary: The only motor nerve of the diaphragm. It runs from the neck down through the chest to the diaphragm and carries sensation from the pericardium, mediastinal pleura and the pleura/peritoneum of the diaphragm.
facts: Cervical plexus – C3, C4, C5 (mainly C4)
Runs down in front of the scalenus anterior, enters the chest between the subclavian artery and vein and passes down the side of the pericardium in front of the lung root to the diaphragm
Diaphragm
Pericardium, mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura, diaphragmatic peritoneum (central part)
clinical: Irritation under the diaphragm (gallbladder, spleen) causes pain referred to the C3–C5 dermatomes, that is, to the shoulder.
After injury the diaphragm on the same side is raised and moves paradoxically.
tus: The right phrenic nerve runs beside the SVC and the right atrium, the left one over the pericardium of the left ventricle.
An accessory phrenic nerve (usually from the nerve to subclavius) can partly keep the diaphragm working after phrenic nerve injury.

n-intercostales.summary: The anterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T11; they supply the muscles and skin of the chest and abdominal wall. The anterior ramus of T12 is called the subcostal nerve.
facts: Anterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T11
Run in the costal groove on the lower border of each rib, below the intercostal artery and vein (VAN); the lower six nerves pass on into the abdominal wall
Intercostal muscles, muscles of the anterior abdominal wall (T7–T12), serratus posterior
Skin of the chest and abdominal wall (dermatomes: T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus)
clinical: Shingles (herpes zoster) causes a painful band-like rash along one intercostal nerve.
In rib fractures an intercostal nerve block relieves the pain.
tus: Most of the first intercostal nerve joins the brachial plexus; the second gives off the intercostobrachial nerve (medial side of the arm).
Intercostal nerves 7–11 supply the abdominal wall (thoracoabdominal nerves).
